title: Where should I start?
answer: Start in Real-data study. Set your original location, landing time in UTC, and surface duration. Enter your terrain, power and communication requirements, then select Search real candidate areas. The search is bounded to the Connecting Ridge study footprint. Open the terrain section to inspect the source maps.

title: Real or simulated data?
answer: Real-data study uses archived NASA LOLA terrain and long-term screening maps with SPICE DE421 geometry for your selected dates. It is not live imagery. NASA percentages describe a long-term modeled cycle, not sunlight hours for your mission. Simulated demo uses fictional sites and illustrative values. Keep those modes distinct.

title: How do comparisons work?
answer: Run a search, then choose Compare R1, R2 or R3. Compare mission sunlight, Earth-hidden intervals, terrain and minimum battery under your entered assumptions. The timeline aligns hours since each landing; the UTC dates can differ. Lower/upper cases express terrain sensitivity, not guaranteed confidence bounds. Earth visibility is only a geometric opportunity, not a proven radio link.

title: Is a qualifying site safe?
answer: Meets assessed limits does not mean safe to land. Ground strength, footpad sinkage, rocks, plume effects, thermal behavior and trajectory reachability remain unassessed. There is no universal best site. This assistant cannot execute searches or choose an optimal site: enter your location, UTC times and requirements in the study form, run the calculator, and review its actual results.

title: What does the terrain map show?
answer: The real study covers a 5 by 5 km Connecting Ridge patch. Switch between NASA sunlight, Earth visibility, permanent shadow and LOLA terrain. Click the map or enter coordinates to set the original point. The hillshade is calculated from elevations, not a photograph. Screening pixels are 60 m; regional elevation is 5 m, and patch checks are 50 m. This does not resolve footpad-scale hazards.

title: Why is the search slow?
answer: A first uncached real-data search can take a minute or more. Wait for its progress indicator; only one analysis runs at a time. Repeating identical inputs can reuse verified cached results. HTTP 429 means the service is busy or a request limit was reached: wait before retrying. If the service is unavailable, use the saved presentation report or the clearly labeled simulated demo.
